tool.name: Strong magnet
tool.measures: the magnetic sensitivity of the stone, linked to its iron content
tips: Put the stone on a smooth surface and bring the magnet close
An ordinary magnet is not enough: you need a very strong magnet
A stone set in a magnetic metal gives a false result

steps.title: Iron attracts the magnet
steps.text: Some stones contain iron (or manganese), and iron reacts to a magnet. With a very strong magnet, you can thus see a stone move or roll towards it.

steps.title: How to do the test
steps.text:
1. Put the stone flat on a smooth surface (or float it on water).
2. Slowly bring the magnet close, without touching it.
3. Watch whether the stone moves, turns or follows the magnet.

The test destroys nothing and takes only a moment.

steps.title: What you observe
steps.text: • Strongly attracted: almandine garnet (very rich in iron). • Attracted: rhodolite, spessartine and demantoid garnets. • Slightly attracted: peridot, hematite, black tourmaline (schorl). • Almost nothing: sapphire, kyanite (traces of iron). • No reaction: most stones, including ruby, emerald and natural diamond.

steps.title: What the test allows
steps.text: The magnet helps tell apart stones that look alike: a red garnet from a ruby, for example. It can also point to a synthetic HPHT diamond, whose growth sometimes leaves tiny remains of metal. But the absence of a reaction proves nothing: you always cross-check with the other instruments.

steps.title: To remember
steps.text: • The magnet reveals the iron contained in the stone. • You need a very strong magnet and a little patience. • The test is one clue among others, quick and harmless for the stone.
